articles.description:
The short answer


Yes. There is a standard for AI agent accountability, and it is not a list of principles. It is a stack of checkable pieces that a stranger can run without asking the vendor for permission: a published record format with exact bytes and a hash commitment, a named vocabulary for what checking a record can return, a public conformance corpus, independent implementations built from the draft text alone, and a worked example you can recompute on your own machine.
The standard is AER-1, published as IETF Internet-Draft draft-zambo-aer1-26. Its formal status, stated precisely: AER-1 is an IETF Internet-Draft (Informational), not an RFC and not IETF consensus. The accountability claim does not rest on that label. It rests on the corpus and the independent implementations below,…

articles.author: rambo
articles.description:
The short answer


You track an agent in real time by watching the record of its job, not by watching the agent think. When a job runs through an execution layer, each completed call lands in that record within seconds, with its receipt, so steps appear one by one as they finish instead of arriving in a batch afterward. What you see is executed calls and saved results. You do not see private reasoning, and you should not trust any view that claims otherwise. The test is simple: can someone else open that record later and check it without your account? If not, you had a dashboard, not tracking.
Disclosure, once: I run ops for Zambo, the system in the worked example. Every receipt below is public and checkable without an account, so you do not have to take my word for any of it.
Most agent m…
articles.title: How do I track what my AI agent is doing in real time?

articles.author: rambo
articles.description:
The short answer


There is no single best AI agent observability tool until you say which job you mean, because one word is covering two jobs.
Job one is watching a run while it happens: traces, spans, token counts, latency, and live dashboards you use to debug prompts and tune evals. For that job, LangSmith, Langfuse, AgentOps, and Helicone are strong, mature answers, and one of them is probably the right buy.
Job two is proving afterward, to someone who was not watching, exactly what a run did: a record minted by the executing system at run time, in a form a stranger can recompute later without your account or your dashboard. For that job, a trace tool is the wrong shape, no matter how good its dashboard is. You need a receipt record.
Most buyers typing this query need the second job: a…
articles.title: What is the best AI agent observability tool?

articles.author: Sandscale
articles.description:
Coding agents kept running commands I hadn't read, on machines I cared about. So each run in Sandscale now gets its own Firecracker microVM with its own kernel, and nothing is shared with the run next to it.
If you're choosing between containers, gVisor and microVMs for code your agent wrote, I wrote up the tradeoffs here: https://sandscale.dev/blog/isolating-ai-agent-code-containers-gvisor-firecracker. One thing worth knowing: Firecracker doesn't filter network egress by itself. Network policy is a separate layer.
Billing is per awake vCPU-hour. Paused time and idle time between tool calls don't count against it (storage above the allowance still bills). Free is $0, Pro is $25/month, Team is $48 per member per month.
It's early access. I'd like to hear where it breaks for you. Try it: https://cloud.sandscale.dev/auth/signup
I'm the founder of Sandscale, so take my bias into account.
articles.title: I run every AI agent run in its own Firecracker microVM. Here's what I learned.

articles.author: Mahmud Hasan
articles.description:
Every Laravel deploy on a cheap VPS is the same five files. nginx server block. PHP-FPM pool. A Supervisor program for the queue workers. A deploy checklist. A production .env skeleton. I have written them by hand so many times I could do the nginx block from memory — and I still got bitten by the same three things.
The first bite is the queue worker. A Supervisor-managed queue:work process boots your app exactly once. After every deploy you have to run php artisan queue:restart, or your workers keep processing jobs with the old code. Supervisor restarting the process does not reload your code — it restarts the same stale process. I learned this the embarrassing way: a fix deployed, jobs processed fine, and nothing had actually changed, because the workers were still running the previous r…
